events/Atlagic-Bosnian-Pasha-Appointment.title: Atlagic-Bosnian-Pasha-Appointment-1687
events/Atlagic-Bosnian-Pasha-Appointment.content:
Atlagić’s Appointment as Bosnian Pasha (early 1687)
In early 1687 Mehmed Atlagić was exempted from a 50,000-real tribute owed to the Grand Vizier in exchange for a promise to return Morlach refugees to the sultan and lead the campaign against Venice as Bosnian pasha (docs 163, 170, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The appointment placed the senior Atlagić of Knin at the head of Ottoman operations in Bosnia until his capture at the fall of Knin in September 1688 (docs 163, 170, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Atlagic-Poison-Attempt-1687.title: Atlagic-Poison-Attempt-1687
events/Atlagic-Poison-Attempt-1687.content:
Senate-Approved Attempt to Poison Atlagić (22 January 1687)
On 22 January 1687 the Inquisitori di Stato sent Girolamo Cornaro poison and instructions for an attempt on the life of Mehmed Atlagić, freshly appointed Bosnian pasha (docs 165, 167, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The plot was either abandoned or failed; a footnote to doc 185 hints that the chaplain duties of frate Andrea (Rama) the next year may have masked a second attempt (docs 165, 167, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Battle-of-Ribnik-1648.title: Battle-of-Ribnik-1648
events/Battle-of-Ribnik-1648.content:
Battle of Ribnik (16–17 July 1648)
Catastrophic defeat of the Kotarski uskoci led by don Stjepan Sorić and harambaše Petar Smiljanić and Janko Mitrović, in their attempt to take the Lika fortress of Ribnik during the early phase of the Candian War.
Casualties (per doc. 38, son Ilija Smiljanić’s deposition; doc. 39, harambaše roster of 14 uskočke grupe)

Killed: don Stjepan Sorić (executed by Turks after capture), Petar Smiljanić, ~10 senior harambaše, ~80 men.
Captured: pop Sorić, then beheaded.
The 14 uskočke grupe roster (doc. 39) lists losses by harambaša with village of origin → settlement village — invaluable for migration mapping (see also doc. 70 1653 proxy).

events/Bjelaj-Migration-1692.title: Bjelaj-Migration-1692
events/Bjelaj-Migration-1692.content:
Bjelaj Migration (March 1692)
5,000 souls migrated from the Bjelaj region (Bosnian frontier near Lika) into Venetian Dalmatia under three serdari — conti Đurić, Pirić, and Zorić — and were settled at:

Plavno (the Bosnian-frontier village near Knin)
Zrmanja
Padene
Mokro-Polje
Oton

(Desnica II, chunk 3.)
Notes

Compared to the 1685 wave (3,051 families / 10,290 fighters under multiple serdari), this 1692 migration is concentrated in Bukovica’s eastern edge and the upper Krka watershed.
Provveditor Alessandro Molin organised the resettlement.
The serdari Đurić, Pirić, and Zorić each enter the wiki as new lineages with this migration; the Đurić brothers Paolo and Vuk are documented (Paolo’s pension transferred to Vuk after his death).

events/Bjelaj-Vakuf-Raid-1685.title: Bjelaj-Vakuf-Raid-1685
events/Bjelaj-Vakuf-Raid-1685.content:
Bjelaj and Vakuf Raid (early September 1685)
Stojan Janković with Tartaglia, Geliseo and Razzetini destroyed the Bjelaj fortress and its Vakuf in early September 1685 and brought back about 500 Orthodox musketeers from Srb to Venetian territory (docs 97, 98, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The raid was a precursor to the larger 1692 Bjelaj migration under conti Đurić, Pirić and Zorić (docs 97, 98, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Border-Demarcation-Grimani-1699-1.title: Border-Demarcation-Grimani-1699-1701
events/Border-Demarcation-Grimani-1699-1.content:
Grimani Border Demarcation — Sfakioto’s Five Processi (1699–1701)
Following the Treaty of Karlowitz, the commission under provveditore generale Grimani (1699–1701) ran Sfakioto’s five processi — extensive testimony-gathering on rights and jurisdiction at Knin, Sinj and Zvonigrad — to fix the new Venetian–Ottoman boundary (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The processi are the principal Venetian dossier on the post-Karlowitz “Acquisto Nuovo” lands and remained authoritative through the 1704 Bukovica revolt and beyond (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Bortulacic-Murder-Vrana-1692.title: Bortulacic-Murder-Vrana-1692
events/Bortulacic-Murder-Vrana-1692.content:
Murder of Šimun Bortulačić at Vrana (16 January 1692)
Šimun (Simon) Bortulačić — kavalier, one of the four 1684 capi de Morlacchi, governor of Vrana — killed at Vrana on 16 January 1692 by men from Biograd and Pakostane; aged ~31; covered with stones (Desnica II, chunk 3 attestations).
Investigation and execution

Two principal perpetrators captured and condemned 1693–94.
The brother of Mattio Žabetić of Zaravecchia was quartered for participation.
Tomaso Tubić (related to Žabetić family) was banished, then later pardoned.
The Žabetić family connection links the 1692 Bortulačić murder to the 1704 Bukovica revolt — Mattio Žabetić, brother of one executed perpetrator, would later be a 1704 ringleader.

Notes

The killing fits the pattern of village-faction violence directed at Venetian-recognised Morlach capi who were exercising sopraintendenza over villages outside their original kin-network. Vrana had earlier rejected Bortulačić as their capo in 1684 (docs 34–36).
Provveditor Daniel Dolfin mediated the broader 1692 settlement of factional feuds in Kotari (Mitrović–Sinobad, Mitrović–Milković reconciliations).

events/Bosnian-Pasha-April-1688-Raid.title: Bosnian-Pasha-April-1688-Raid
events/Bosnian-Pasha-April-1688-Raid.content:
Bosnian Pasha’s April 1688 Raid on Kotari
About 5,000 Bosnian cavalry under Atlagić crossed via Livno and Knin to Popovići in April 1688 and plundered the Kotari plain from Nadin to Novigrad (docs 198, 200, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The raiders took 23 heads, 4,000–5,000 small animals, 600 horses/cattle and roughly 100 women and children captive; Karin defended itself successfully (docs 198, 200, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II). The raid was Atlagić’s last large-scale offensive before Venice took Knin that September.

events/Bosnian-Pasha-Kotari-Raid-1686.title: Bosnian-Pasha-Kotari-Raid-1686
events/Bosnian-Pasha-Kotari-Raid-1686.content:
Bosnian Pasha’s Raid on Kotari (12–19 November 1686)
About 16,000 Turks under five pashas, supported by 6-pounder cannon, descended from Knin onto the Kotari plain between 12 and 19 November 1686 (docs 149–157, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The raiders burned the straw houses of Bribir, Ostrovica, Velim and Kožulovo polje; Vrana and Perušić defended themselves and held (docs 149–157, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II). It was the largest Ottoman counter-strike on the Kotari during the Morean War, retaliation for the Venetian conquest of Sinj two months earlier.

events/Bribir-Ambush-1668.title: Bribir-Ambush-1668
events/Bribir-Ambush-1668.content:
Zaseda na bribirskom potoku (9 December 1668)
Set-piece ambush by 200 horse + 200 foot of Kotarci (under Stojan Janković, Smoljan Smiljanić and Giovanni Battista Soppe Fortezza) of a 120-strong elite Knin Turkish raiding party led by Ibraim aga Kovačević. After provveditor Priuli’s intelligence, Soppe led the main column from Nadin to the Bribir torrent and trapped the returning Turks at the river crossing.
Turkish casualties: ~104 killed (only 15 Turks escaped on horseback). Venetian-side: 1 dead. 66 saddled cavalry captured. Senate awarded Soppe + Smiljanić + Mitrović gold rings (doc. 165, 1669-01-02).
The Bribir potok had previously been the site of Vuk Močivuna’s death (1666), and the Morlachi explicitly framed this 1668 victory as vendetta for that earlier defeat.
Source
Desnica-1950-Kotarski-Uskoci-I — doc. 163 (Priuli’s dispatch, 18 Dec 1668), doc. 165 (Senate’s reply, 2 Jan 1669).

events/Brochno-Goranci-Migration-1693-94.title: Brochno-Goranci-Migration-1693-94
events/Brochno-Goranci-Migration-1693-94.content:
Brochno–Blato–Goranci Migration (1693–1694)
About 5,000 souls from the Brochno–Blato–Goranci villages (Hercegovina) crossed onto Venetian territory in 1693–1694 under five serdari and 22 harambasse, settling around Zadvarje and Vrgorac (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The migration is among the largest single transfers documented for the post-1690 phase of the Morean War in lower Dalmatia, alongside the 1692 Bjelaj migration and the Rašić migration of the same year (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Bukovica-Revolt-1704.title: Bukovica-Revolt-1704
events/Bukovica-Revolt-1704.content:
Bukovica Revolt (1702–1704)
A revolt in the Bukovica part of the Zadar contado against tax-collection abuse, decima reform, and troop quartering, suppressed in summer 1704 by Provveditor Generale Marin Zane.
Origins (1702)
Per pop Petar Jagodić-Kuridža’s long deposition (doc 389, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II):

Colonel Antonio Canagetti (dragoons) demanded 300 zecchini from the parish of San Pietro in Bokovica via mandate of provveditor Zane.
The commune denied the debt; Jagodić drafted a four-point petition for the commune asking instead:

Voiding of the 300-zecchini claim
Restitution of 100 manzi previously usurped by colonel Posedarski
Reform of decima collection (decimario refusing in-cash payment, requiring instead a 60-dragoon entourage at communal cost)
Permission to pay decima in wheat at communal expense delivery


Provveditor Zane assented in part; ordered Posedarski to pay the 100 manzi back and Canagetti to drop the 300 zecchini claim.

Escalation
Posedarski, summoned, lured 30 capi to Zerno on pretence of payment, then refused to pay and threatened to hang a dozen of them. The commune resolved to send three capi to Venice via the dominante.
Suppression (1704)

Banishment with capital sentence of three commune capi and pop Jagodić.
Capi fled to imperial Lika.
Mattio Žabetić of Zaravecchia arrested in Venice 1704.
Pop Jagodić arrested under successor provveditor Vincenzo Vendramin, taken to Klin (Cliuno?), then Venetian Pozzi prison.
The three banished capi liberated 1715 in War of Spanish Succession amnesty.

Resolution

1746-03-29 — Pop Jagodić, blind, deaf, and crippled by ~40 years’ imprisonment, freed by State Inquisitors and entrusted to the Greek Petar Spiro in Venice (doc 390).
1749-04-09 — Jagodić dies, age 80, entered in matica umrlih of Sv. Ilija (Greek-rite) parish, Zadar (doc 392).

Co-leaders documented

pop Petar Jagodić-Kuridža — parish priest of Sv. Petar, Bokovica.
Ilija Nanić of Žegar.
Mattio Žabetić of Zaravecchia (whose brother was earlier quartered for the Bortulačić murder of 1692).

Notes

The revolt was partial breakdown of the Pertinenze framework of 1689 — the colonel Posedarski’s misuse of his pertinenza authority, combined with the dragoon decimal-collection regime, generated the grievance.
The 40-year imprisonment of Jagodić without trial is one of the more striking documents in the volume — Desnica reproduces both his 1746 deposition and the State Inquisitors’ release order in full.

events/Bunjevac-Migration-to-Backa-c1606.title: Bunjevac-Migration-to-Backa-c1606
events/Bunjevac-Migration-to-Backa-c1606.content:
Bunjevac migrations to Bačka (c. 1554 – c. 1622)
Ottoman-administered transfers of “buntovni vlaški element” from Sandzak-Klis / Sandzak-Krka into the depopulated Budim eyalet (Bačka, Baranja). Documented in three layers Saric-2008-Bunjevci:
1. Earliest layer (c. 1530–1582)

1530s — Ottoman deportations of rebellious Vlachs from Vilajet-Hrvati to Podunavlje (cited in 1564–65 ferman).
1554 — Mohač defter, selo Márok (Baranja): rajetin Marton-Bunavac-b????-Marok (“Márton Bunavácz”). Earliest possible written form of “Bunjevac” Saric-2008-Bunjevci (caveats: possibly a transcription error for Dunavac; possibly an etnik attached to a non-Bunjevac).
1561 — same person registered in nearby selo Izsép as “Martin Bunivac”.
1581 — knez Vranes-Ivanovic-b????-Kaloca with a knežina near Kaloča.
1582 — Bosnian Franciscan Anto-Matkovic-b???? opens a school for “Dalmatince” in the Temišvar diocese.
1554 + 1561 deftere also register raja designated “Hirvat” (regional Croat from former vilajet Hrvati) in selo Sukit and selo Ata (Šarošac 1991).

2. Main wave (1606–1620) — after the Long War
After 1598, ~15,000 Serbs from the bajska/somborska/subotička nahija migrated north to the Ostrogon area at Pálffy’s invitation. Ottoman authorities backfilled with Bunjevac groups from Sandzak-Klis Saric-2008-Bunjevci:

1608 — Šibenik knez reports to Venetian senate that 2,000 morlačkih kuća were transferred across the Danube.
1608+ — fallout of the Drniš revolt under Mehmed-Terzibasic-b????-Drnis.
1619 — further Klis-area Vlach migrations including Orthodox Vlachs going with Dragović monastery monks to Grabovac in Baranja.
1622 — first explicit “parochia Bunievczi” attestation: don Simun-Matkovic-b???? addresses a request to the Congregatio Propaganda Fide for the Bunjevac parish in the Kalocsa archdiocese.
1626 — Athanasio Georgiceo records: “raja for 25 years has fled Klis sandžak; population dropped from 30,000 houses to 20,000.”

3. Toponymic and linguistic evidence

Mid-17th-c. settlement names along the Krivaja near Subotica show clearly Dinaric origin: Kupuszina, Stanišić, Zobnatica.
Dragović monastery near Cetina founded the orthodox monastery Grabovac in Baranja in 1585.

Motivation
Šarić frames these as ambivalent: nominally Ottoman kaznene deportacije, but for the Bunjevci themselves often a welcome escape from the “tatarska dinastija” of Klis sandžak-begs (Mustafa-beg-Klis-b???? and his son Mehmed-beg-Klis-b????, both Tatar-origin) and the Memibegović dynasty of Sandzak-Krka.

events/Cetina-Migration-Peraica-1685.title: Cetina-Migration-Peraica-1685
events/Cetina-Migration-Peraica-1685.content:
Cetina Morlach Migration under Peraica (March 1685)
Ilija Peraica led roughly 600 armed men with their families plus 30,000 small animals and 10,000 cattle from Cetina into Trogir territory under Venetian protection (docs 59–66, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The migration shifted the Cetina Morlach population from Ottoman to Venetian allegiance and supplied a new manpower pool for the campaigns in lower Dalmatia later that year (docs 59–66, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Cetina-Rotta-1666.title: Cetina-Rotta-1666
events/Cetina-Rotta-1666.content:
Cetinska rotta (5 April 1666)
Disastrous defeat of the Šibenik-Zadar Morlach raiding force (under serdar Cvitan Šarić, with Janković Stojan and many Šibenik harambaše) on the Cetina river near Obrovac na Cetini, half a day’s march from Klis, when the čiehaja of the Bosnian basha caught them with cavalry mid-plunder.
Casualties

~200 Kotarci dead and captured.
Stojan Janković captured — beginning his 14-month slavery in Constantinople.
Per witnesses (docs. 149, 150) and Cornaro’s dispatch (doc. 148): the vecchio, ardito e pieno d’ avidità serdar Cvitan Šarić had concerted the raid against orders.
Turkish casualties also heavy: alai-beg Atlagić killed; aga Baraković killed; Cinghić (Čengić) mortally wounded.

Source
Desnica-1950-Kotarski-Uskoci-I — docs. 148–151 (Cornaro’s dispatch + 3 depositions + Mihovil Družeić’s report from Cetina).

events/Coron-Conquest-1685.title: Coron-Conquest-1685
events/Coron-Conquest-1685.content:
Venetian Conquest of Koroni (1685)
Venetian forces took Koroni (Coron) in the Morea in 1685, an early signal victory of the Morean War (doc 100, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The success in the Morea was the strategic counterpart to the Dalmatian campaigns of Stojan Janković and the four Kotari capi the same season (doc 100, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Crna-Gora-Defection-1685.title: Crna-Gora-Defection-1685
events/Crna-Gora-Defection-1685.content:
Montenegrin Tribes’ Defection to Skadar Sandžak (May 1685)
Parts of the Montenegrin tribes joined the Sandžak-beg of Skadar against Venice in May 1685, reversing the cooperative posture that had begun the Morean War (doc 72, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The defection complicated Venetian operations on the southern Adriatic flank for the rest of the war (doc 72, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Cyprus-War-1570-1573.title: Cyprus-War-1570-1573
events/Cyprus-War-1570-1573.content:
Cyprus War (1570–1573)
Ottoman capture of Zemunik, Učitelja Vas, and Tinj in northern Dalmatia. Triggered new Vlach defections to Venetian Dalmatia and Istria, though land shortage at Zadar limited reception Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre. After the war, Ferhat-beg-Sokolovic-b???? uvakufio Tinj for the Zemunik vakuf and brought western-Hercegovinian Vlach colonists (Vojnic, later “Bunjevci”). Period sees the final replacement of “Vlasi Istre” identity by new Vlach demographic streams from southeastern Dinarides.

events/Esztergom-Battle-1685.title: Esztergom-Battle-1685
events/Esztergom-Battle-1685.content:
Battle of Esztergom (1685)
The Imperial army under Charles V, Duke of Lorraine defeated the Ottomans at Esztergom in 1685; some 2,000 Turks were killed and 25 cannon captured (doc 95, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The Imperial Hungarian victories of 1685 ran in parallel with the Venetian Dalmatian offensive — the Holy League’s two-front assault on the Ottoman Empire after the failed siege of Vienna in 1683 (doc 95, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Glamoc-Engagement-1686.title: Glamoc-Engagement-1686
events/Glamoc-Engagement-1686.content:
Glamoč Cavalry Engagement (early summer 1686)
A Kotari sortie cut down roughly 200 Turkish cavalry on the Glamoč field in early summer 1686 (doc 138, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The clash kept the Glamoč–Livno corridor open for the larger raids of July and September that year (doc 138, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Glamoc-Grahovo-Campaign-1684.title: Glamoc-Grahovo-Campaign-1684
events/Glamoc-Grahovo-Campaign-1684.content:
Glamoč–Grahovo Campaign (August 1684)
Some 5,000 Morlachs under Janković, Smiljanić and Bortulačić raided Glamoč, burning the palaces of alajbeg Filipović and killing 50 Turks (docs 27, 30, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
On the return march they ambushed two Bosnian-Hercegovinian pashas (one identified as Mazut-paša) at Grahovo: 150 Turks were killed including 30 court agas and two “Bugliuch bassé”; one pasha was wounded; Sinovčić cut down the pasha’s kjehaja (docs 27, 30, 32, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II). Smiljanić was lightly wounded in the hand; no Morlach deaths reported (docs 27, 30, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Grusi-Krajiski-Statut-1654.title: Grusi-Krajiski-Statut-1654
events/Grusi-Krajiski-Statut-1654.content:
Krajiški statut iz Grusi (5 August 1654)
The earliest surviving Kotarska “liga” (krajiški) statute — passed at a Krajina-wide assembly at Grusi on 5 August 1654, attended by the gospodin serdar sa svim vojvodami i suci. Italian translation by Đorđe Đerolim Đordani (cancelliere della lettera illirica e serviana) appended to the Bosnian-Cyrillic original.
9 capitoli

od potoči: when called to chase the Turks, missing the muster = 50 libre fine.
od ubojstva: accidental killing → 300 groša to the liga + cost of potroški.
od lupeža (theft): horse / ox / sheep / hen / sheaf / other goods → 1 head returned to owner + 6 heads to liga.
prodaja, krađa, jatak: full liga punishes traitors and accomplices.
Disobedience to one’s sudac or kapetan = 25 libre.
Drawing a weapon at the sbor / in army / in town = 10 groša for sword/musket.
od neprijatelja plivo zaiao: failure to chase a fleeing enemy = 7-fold restitution.
Trampled meadow — same penalty as wheat.
Failure to come to a lumbarda (cannon-warning) = 5 tolari to the liga.

Signed: “Ovo pisa sva Kraina s licenciom gosposkom. Gospodin serdar sa svim voivodami i suci učiniše, i svi ovomuh kuntenti biše.” + “Ovo učini sva Kraina gorjna i dojna do Pakoštana.”
Source
Desnica-1950-Kotarski-Uskoci-I — doc. 85 (Zadarski stari arhiv, Spisi G. A. Zen, knj. II, str. 121).

events/Ilija-Bilaj-Raid-1687.title: Ilija-Bilaj-Raid-1687
events/Ilija-Bilaj-Raid-1687.content:
Ilija’s Raid on Bilaj (June 1687)
Ilija Mitrović led 800 men, including 400 cavalry, in a raid on the Bilaj tower in June 1687; the captain of Bilaj lost his brother and son in the engagement (doc 170, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The raid paralleled his brother Zaviša’s Rebac raid and prefigured the disastrous family expedition to Duvno two months later in which their elder brother Stojan would be killed (doc 170, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Jankovic-Regiment-Authorisation-1.title: Jankovic-Regiment-Authorisation-1686
events/Jankovic-Regiment-Authorisation-1.content:
Authorisation of Stojan Janković’s oltramarino regiment (7 Nov 1686)
By dukal of 7 November 1686 (doc 148, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II), Doge Marc’Antonio Giustinian authorised a 500-strong oltramarino regiment under the command of kavalier Stojan Janković, with his older son Nikola designated as colonnello, and younger son Konstantin designated as head of an attached cavalry company.
By 21 November 1686 Janković had assembled 300 men toward the regiment in Zadar (doc 158). Captains of the regiment included Nikola Blagojević (Šibenik), Jovan Božić (Zadar), and others recommended by vice-commissario Antonio Molin (doc 158).
The regiment marked a major institutional elevation of the Janković family from harambaše/sardari of Morlach contingents to commanders of a regular paid Venetian unit.
Notes

Stojan was killed at Duvno in August 1687 (doc 174); Nikola died in the Levant ~1687/early 1688; only Konstantin survived among the named sons.

events/Kanjiza-Raid-1688.title: Kanjiza-Raid-1688
events/Kanjiza-Raid-1688.content:
Kotarci Raid on Kanjiža (April 1688)
About 300 Kotarci under Kalinić rode out from Korlat in April 1688 against Kanjiža and took 50 captives, 4,000 small animals and 500 large (doc 202, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
On the return the raiders were intercepted by 100 cavalry under Dukajtar and lost 15–20 dead (doc 202, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Karlovacki-Mir-1699.title: Karlovacki-Mir-1699
events/Karlovacki-Mir-1699.content:
Karlovački mir (1699)
Treaty ending the Great Turkish War; recovered Lika and Krbava for the Habsburgs.
The Habsburg boundary commission was led by count Luigi-Marsigli-b????. In commission documents, Marsigli refers to the Bunjevci of the Primorska Krajina as “Meerkroaten” (Sea-Croats) — his term for the predominantly Bunjevac population of the Senjska-Kapetanija coastline at the turn of the 18th c. (Kaser 2003) Saric-2008-Bunjevci.

events/Kastela-Attack-1685.title: Kastela-Attack-1685
events/Kastela-Attack-1685.content:
Ottoman Attack on Kaštela (early April 1685)
About 3,000 cavalry under Ahmed-paša of Hercegovina struck Kaštela near Split in early April 1685, but were repulsed by some 3,000 castellani and Morlach defenders (doc 62, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Mustafa Jasko was captured during the engagement; the attack came simultaneously with the Venetian disaster at Sinj and was the southern prong of a coordinated Ottoman counter-offensive in spring 1685 (doc 62, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Klis-Conquest-1648.title: Klis-Conquest-1648
events/Klis-Conquest-1648.content:
Osvajanje Klisa (1648)
Venetian campaign that conquered Drniš, Klis, and (briefly) Knin from Tekieli Mustafa-paša, who personally led the relief but was defeated at Greben outside Klis. Foscolo’s terminacija (doc. 26, 1648-04-20) gives the most detailed published account of pop Sorić’s role.
Sorić’s role

Cut bridges; burned Zvonigrad mills and folli; shifted Bukovački Morlachi by force.
Helped force the Cikola crossing toward Drniš under Tekieli’s defending fire.
At Drniš seized Tekieli’s general standard (later sent to Venice in triumph).
At Klis — held the Greben pass; broke Tekieli’s advance at Dugopolje.
16-day siege of Klis ended in Venetian capture.

Source
Desnica-1950-Kotarski-Uskoci-I — doc. 26.

events/Knin-Battle-1684.title: Knin-Battle-1684
events/Knin-Battle-1684.content:
Battle of Knin (2 June 1684)
Roughly 2,000 Kotari Morlachs under Stojan Janković, Smoljan Smiljanić and Antun Bortulačić fell on the Knin garrison; about 120 Turks were killed and ~90 horses captured (doc 9, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Janković was lightly wounded. The action was the first joint sortie of the four Kotari capi after Vrana’s defection and signalled an offensive Morlach posture in the opening months of the Morean War (doc 9, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Knin-Conquest-1688.title: Knin-Conquest-1688
events/Knin-Conquest-1688.content:
Conquest of Knin (29 August – 11 September 1688)
Provveditor Generale Girolamo Cornaro’s 15-day siege of Knin: assault on the city 2 September; siege of the inner fortresses; surrender on 11 September by Mehmed pasha Atlagić “to discretion” (docs 213–220, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Atlagić, his son Mehmed-beg Atlagić, and his nephew Alibeg Atlagić (“la più brava spada”) were all captured.
The conquest secured the Krka–Cetina interior and the entire frontage from Knin to Vrlika. Vrlika capitulated without a shot to colonnello Fenzi in early September 1688 (doc 216); Bože Cerniza was placed as garrison commander. The conquest of Knin and Vrlika together complete the Venetian recovery of the Cetina–Krka basin begun with Sinj 1686.
Wider context (August 1688)

Imperial victory at Brod / crossing of the Sava (early Aug 1688) — Bosnian pasha defeated
Imperial siege of Gradiška, ~12,000 Imperial troops near Belgrade (doc 211)
The combined Holy League pressure made Bosnian relief of Knin impossible

events/Knin-Millworks-Raid-1686.title: Knin-Millworks-Raid-1686
events/Knin-Millworks-Raid-1686.content:
Knin Millworks Raid (June 1686)
Stojan Janković led a raid that destroyed 25–29 mills along the Krka above Knin together with a defensive tower in June 1686 (doc 135, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Crippling the Knin mills targeted the garrison’s grain supply and prepared the ground for the eventual conquest of Knin two summers later (doc 135, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Kotari-Pertinenze-Reform-1689.title: Kotari-Pertinenze-Reform-1689
events/Kotari-Pertinenze-Reform-1689.content:
Kotari Pertinenze Reform (11 March 1689)
By ordinance of Girolamo Cornaro (doc 224, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II), the territory of Zadar was divided into 9 administrative pertinenze (units), each under a named governor and a dedicated league of judges. The reform regulated:

Descrizione rules (the Venetian land-population census)
Agricultural rights (pasturage, ploughing, cultivation of abandoned Ottoman lands)
Decime (tithe) collection procedures
Militia rolls — every village to know its capi and its mobilisation strength

The reform formalised the patchwork of sopraintendenze the four Morlach capi had held informally since 1684 (Posedarski, Bortulačić, Janković, Smiljanić) plus the four Mocenigo “new” capi (Soppe brothers, Ventura, Alberti). Following the deaths of Stojan Janković (1687), Smoljan Smiljanić (by 1689), and the elder Posedarski brothers, the reform was also a generational handoff — the new colonnello Frane Posedarski is identified in the ordinance as “figlio e nipote respective de medemi” (son of one, nephew of the other).
The Liga statute was reissued by Daniel Dolfin on 12 February 1696 (doc later in series).
Notes

This is the foundational governance instrument of the Venetian Ravni Kotari for the rest of the Republic’s tenure (until 1797). All later Venetian administrators worked within or amended this framework.
The Mitrović–Sinobad and Mitrović–Milković reconciliations of 1692 (under Dolfin) operate within the pertinenze framework; the 1704 Bukovica revolt is a partial breakdown of it.

events/Krmpote-Migration-Lic-1605.title: Krmpote-Migration-Lic-1605
events/Krmpote-Migration-Lic-1605.content:
First Krmpote migration to Lič (1605)
First major migration of the Vlasi Krmpote from Ottoman territory in the Bukovica/Obrovac area (selo Medvidja, formerly “Krmpote”) onto Habsburg territory, settling Lic on the Zrinski estate of Hreljin Saric-2008-Bunjevci.
Family list (Pavličević 1989)
24 surnames in the 1605 group, mostly Krmpote core but including some Vojnic and Sladovic families:
Krmpote (24 families):
Balinović (Balen), Barulovic, Bozic, Budisalic, Butorčić (Butorac), Cvitic, Draganovic, Hromic, Kovac, Krivalica, Krmpotic, Krnjac, Malovridnjak, Matijevic, Markovic, Mihovilovic, Mikulic, Miletic, Oprokovic, Pecanic, Petrovic, Skorupović (Skorup), Simunovic, Vukoslavic.
Vojnići (15 families):
Božić, Galešić, Jurjevic, Matijević, Pavlicic, Petkovic, Stojcevic, Vojnić, Vojnović.
Sladovići — “Gvozdenovi ljudi” (20 families) under Gvozden-Sladovic-b????-Mostar:
Balinović, Broskovic, Ilnic, Karanovic, Lovric, Martinovic, Mihovilović, Mikulić, Sladovic, Veljanic, Vilenica.
Confessional note
Some Orthodox families joined the migration; absent of Orthodox infrastructure in Lič area, they fully Catholicized within a century. By ~1700 the Krmpoćani were a homogeneous Catholic community Saric-2008-Bunjevci.
Confidence
Surname list reconstructed from Pavličević 1989 (compiled from later 18th-c. records). Treat names as medium confidence — plausible but not register-direct.

events/Krmpote-Migration-Lic-1627.title: Krmpote-Migration-Lic-1627
events/Krmpote-Migration-Lic-1627.content:
Second Krmpote migration to Lič (1627)
Second wave of Krmpote families from Ottoman territory onto Habsburg Lic Saric-2008-Bunjevci. No surviving register; family list reconstructed by Pavličević 1989 by comparison with the 1605 settler population (any 1712 Lič Bunjevac surname not in the 1605 list).
Reconstructed family list (16 families)
Blazevic, Deranja, Filipovic, Jovanovic, Krpan, Pavelic, Pavlicevic, Pericic, Prpic, Radosevic, Starcevic, Sojat, Tomic, Tomičić, Tomljanovic, Vukelic.
Confidence
Medium — reconstruction, not register-direct. The list is methodologically sound but no 1627 document survives.

events/Krmpote-Migration-Vinjerac-1647.title: Krmpote-Migration-Vinjerac-1647
events/Krmpote-Migration-Vinjerac-1647.content:
Krmpote migration to Vinjerac (1647)
Final mass exodus of Krmpote families from Ottoman territory during the Candian War. Harambaša Harambasa-Njegovan-b????-Medvidja led 40–50 Krmpote families from selo Krmpote (today Medvidja) to Venetian territory, settling primarily Vinjerac and Starigrad in the Zadar district; some onward to the island of Pag Saric-2008-Bunjevci.
In the same year, the Vlasi Vojnići crossed entirely to Venetian territory under knez Filip-Zupanovic-b????-Tinj, with part of them resettled at Valtura near Pula in southern Istria.
This is the last large group movement out of the Ottoman Bukovica/Tinj area; by 1647 the Krmpote and Vojnić katuns are functionally split between Venetian and Habsburg territories.

events/Lapac-Raid-1686.title: Lapac-Raid-1686
events/Lapac-Raid-1686.content:
Lapac Raid (early January 1686)
Stojan Janković led 1,250 Morlachs into the Lapac region in early January 1686, burning the Pašić palazzo at Boričevac and capturing Idris-aga of Bihać (doc 118, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The raid extended the Morlach offensive far into Bosnian Krajina territory in mid-winter and was followed by larger campaigns deeper into Bosnia later that year (doc 118, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Lika-Bunjevac-Colonization-1690.title: Lika-Bunjevac-Colonization-1690
events/Lika-Bunjevac-Colonization-1690.content:
Bunjevac colonization of Lika–Krbava (1690+)
Major influx of Bunjevac families from coastal Senjska Krajina (Krmpote-Senj, Krivi-Put, Ledenice, Senjska-Draga, Sv-Jakov) and from Venetian territory (Vinjerac, Starigrad, Pag) into recovered Lika–Krbava after the Habsburg expulsion of the Ottomans.
Settlement nuclei: Pazariste, Smiljan, Lovinac Saric-2008-Bunjevci.
Notable settlers

Porkulab Milos-Starcevic-b1656-Veliki-Zitnik settles Pazariste in 1690; per the 1712 popis (Kaser 2003) holds 168 štrikova in Pazarište / Vaganac / Veliki-Zitnik with one son Jakov (age ~20) and 5 other family members.
Rukavine receive estates in Sv-Mihovil, Sv-Rok, Vratnik, Ricice, Kosinj in 1691 (per Fras 1835).

1712 popis (Kaser 2003)
First systematic register: ~158 Bunjevac surnames counted across 23 Lika/Otočac/Ogulin parishes. 37 surnames are shared between Catholic Bunjevci and Orthodox Vlasi — common Dinaric origin documented Saric-2008-Bunjevci (see footnote 58 of the article).
Bunjevac priests at major Bunjevac parishes in 1712:

Lovinac — Damjan-Zdunic-b????-Lovinac (the pop Zduna of folk tradition)
Novo — Petar-Butkovic-b????-Novo
Smiljan — Simun-Zdunic-b????-Smiljan
Pazarište — Juraj-Smolcic-b????-Pazariste

The katoličko svećenstvo was led by Marko-Mesic-b????-Lika during the popis.
This colonization seeds the “ličko-primorska” Bunjevac branch that culminates a century later in the Starčević political dynasty.

events/Lika-Joint-Raid-1685.title: Lika-Joint-Raid-1685
events/Lika-Joint-Raid-1685.content:
Joint Lika Raid by the Four Capi (22 July 1685)
The four capi — Posedarski, Bortulačić, Janković and Smiljanić — raided across Lika hitting Rebac, Ribnik, Medak, Parčići, Tepsincich, Pavlocich and Komić on 22 July 1685 (docs 86, 87, 89, 90, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
About 300 Morlach houses were resettled onto Venetian territory as a result of the raid (docs 86, 87, 89, 90, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Lika-Migration-May-1685.title: Lika-Migration-May-1685
events/Lika-Migration-May-1685.content:
Lika Migration under Janković (May 1685)
Stojan Janković brought 70 Lika families — about 900 souls — onto Venetian territory under the authority of provveditore Polo Michiel (doc 70, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The transfer continued the trickle of Lika refugees that swelled into the Imperial-Venetian competition for settlers behind the 1685 settlement census (doc 70, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Lika-Settlement-Census-1685.title: Lika-Settlement-Census-1685
events/Lika-Settlement-Census-1685.content:
Lika Settlement Census (1685)
Aggregate Venetian census of Morlachs newly settled from Ottoman territory into the Venetian Kotari–Bukovica–Cetina–Neretva line over 1684–85, drawn together in doc 107 (Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Totals (per doc 107)

3,051 families / 10,290 fighters total

Component contingents

1,587 families / 5,297 fighters under Stojan Janković (Lika + Srb)
52 families / 171 fighters under Smoljan Smiljanić
109 families / 283 fighters under Šimun Bortulačić
(no separate count) under Frane Posedarski
140 families / 340 fighters at Vrana
95 families / 255 fighters in Primorje
550 families / 2,300 fighters at Zadvarje + Župa
94 families / 120 fighters at the Neretva (Narenta)
24 families / 124 fighters at Forte Opus
400 families / 1,400 fighters under “Peraica” (Cetina migration of March 1685, Frane Peraica / Ilija Peraica)

Earlier roll-ups feeding the total

1684 (May–Aug): 152 families / 2,300 souls from Lika (doc 8)
1685-05: 70 families / 900 souls under Polo Michiel via Janković (doc 70)
1685-06: 316 families / 2,561 souls settled between Kožulovo polje and Ostrovica (doc 73, 90)

Notes

The 1685 settlement is the single largest Morlach migration into Venetian Dalmatia of the Morean War.
Settlement was unstable: many of the Šibenik- and Trogir-territory new Morlachs were known to be in correspondence with Livno Turks about returning, and the November 1686 pasha raid tested the new settlements severely.
Many of the Lika-origin surnames in the Kotari date from this 1684–85 wave; the 1692 Bjelaj migration (5,000 souls under serdari Đurić, Pirić, Zorić) added a second wave.

events/Livno-Raid-First-1686.title: Livno-Raid-First-1686
events/Livno-Raid-First-1686.content:
First Livno Raid (mid-July 1686)
About 5,000 infantry and 1,500 cavalry under the four Kotari serdars — Posedarski, Bortulačić, Janković and Smiljanić — struck the Livno field in mid-July 1686 (doc 136, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Some 400+ Turks were killed and roughly 1,800 houses burned across the polje (doc 136, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II). A second, smaller Livno raid followed two months later — see Livno-Raid-Second-1686.

events/Livno-Raid-Second-1686.title: Livno-Raid-Second-1686
events/Livno-Raid-Second-1686.content:
Second Livno Raid (early September 1686)
Janković and Smiljanić led a follow-up raid on the Livno field in early September 1686 in which 150+ Turks were killed (docs 141, 142, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
On the return march Karalija and two captains were killed by the pursuit, marking a costly Morlach loss to set against the Livno gains (docs 141, 142, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Mikiel-Knin-Reconnaissance-1685.title: Mikiel-Knin-Reconnaissance-1685
events/Mikiel-Knin-Reconnaissance-1685.content:
Mikiel’s Knin Reconnaissance (February 1685)
A 600-strong Venetian force under provveditore Mikiel, with Stojan Janković and Smoljan Smiljanić, burned outlying houses around Knin while only 8 Turkish horses were watering at the river; 4 Turks were captured (doc 51, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The reconnaissance demonstrated that Knin was vulnerable but a full assault on it would not come until 1688 (doc 51, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Mitrovic-Sinobad-Reconciliation-1.title: Mitrovic-Sinobad-Reconciliation-1692
events/Mitrovic-Sinobad-Reconciliation-1.content:
Mitrović–Sinobad Reconciliation (March 1692)
In March 1692 Provveditore Generale Daniel Dolfin mediated a reconciliation between the Mitrović and Milković parties; an oath was sworn in church and the long-running feud (engami implacable) between the Mitrović house and the Sinobad house was also formally resolved (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
To keep the families apart Jovan Sinobad moved his household from Posedarje to Knin (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II). The Mitrović–Sinobad krvarina had been documented as far back as 1684 among the Budin Morlachs.

events/Mostar-Mokro-Polje-Raid-1696.title: Mostar-Mokro-Polje-Raid-1696
events/Mostar-Mokro-Polje-Raid-1696.content:
Selman Pasha’s Raid on Mokro Polje (~1696)
While Provveditore Generale Daniel Dolfin was at Ulcinj in 1696, Selman pasha of Mostar struck Mokro-Polje but was repulsed by Jovan Sinobad (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
About 100 Turks were killed and 100 enslaved; Sinobad’s nephew was killed in the action (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Mostar-Rusic-Migration-1692.title: Mostar-Rusic-Migration-1692
events/Mostar-Rusic-Migration-1692.content:
Mostar / Rašić Migration to Makarska (1692)
Ivan Rašić led roughly 200 souls (about 25 families) out of the Mostar area onto Venetian territory in 1692; they settled at Zavojane, Stigli and Hadži Lukovo in the Makarska hinterland (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Companion to the Bjelaj migration of the same year and to the larger Brochno–Blato–Goranci transfer of 1693–1694 (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Neuhausel-Capture-1685.title: Neuhausel-Capture-1685
events/Neuhausel-Capture-1685.content:
Imperial Capture of Nové Zámky / Neuhäusel (1685)
The fortress of Neuhäusel (Nové Zámky) in Upper Hungary was taken by Imperial assault in 1685, eliminating one of the principal Ottoman strongholds in the kingdom (doc 95, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The fall of Neuhäusel and the Esztergom victory together marked the decisive turn of the Hungarian campaign in 1685 (doc 95, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Olib-Sale-1701.title: Olib-Sale-1701
events/Olib-Sale-1701.content:
Olib Sale — Half-Island to Mitrović (1701)
In 1701 conte Giacomo Califfi transferred half of the island of Olib (near Pag) to the Mitrović family for 8,000 ducats, with peculiar dynastic conditions: the half-share was to remain perpetually divided between the male line of Zaviša Janković and the male line of his deceased brother Ilija (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The arrangement is one of the few documented Mitrović land acquisitions outside the Zadar mainland and codified the joint Zaviša/Ilija inheritance pattern that would shape the family’s 18th-century landholdings (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Ottoman-Conquest-of-Croatia-1522-.title: Ottoman-Conquest-of-Croatia-1522-1527
events/Ottoman-Conquest-of-Croatia-1522-.content:
Ottoman Conquest of Croatia (1522–1527)
Decisive Ottoman push into central Croatia, ~12,000 km² conquered. Old Croatian župe and noble communities, “banska zemlja” (Banadego), and Krbava knežstvo destroyed; Knin and Krbava-Modruš dioceses reduced to titular sees Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre. Conquered area organized as Vilajet Hrvati under sandžak Bosna, with Gazi Husrev-beg as sanjakbeg and Murat-beg Gajdić as subaša/vojvoda. Triggered the first major Vlach refugee migration northwest into Istria and Kras.

events/Papal-Anti-Pirate-Recruitment-171.title: Papal-Anti-Pirate-Recruitment-1717
events/Papal-Anti-Pirate-Recruitment-171.content:
Papal Anti-Pirate Recruitment of Morlachs (1717)
Cardinal Paulucci, Secretary of State of Pope Clement XI, requested 300 Morlachs from Venice in 1717 to serve aboard papal galliots in the anti-piracy campaign in the Adriatic and Mediterranean (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The request is among the earliest documented uses of Kotari Morlachs in extra-Venetian service and presages the Morlach companies that fought in 18th-century Italian theatres (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Pastrovici-Siege-Relief-1686.title: Pastrovici-Siege-Relief-1686
events/Pastrovici-Siege-Relief-1686.content:
Relief of Paštrovići Towers (March 1686)
A Venetian galeotta under Corponese broke the Ottoman blockade of the Paštrovići towers in March 1686 and resupplied the besieged garrisons (doc 131, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The action stabilised the Venetian outposts on the Montenegrin coast after the Montenegrin defection of May 1685 (doc 131, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Patriarch-Crnojevic-Teodosije-169.title: Patriarch-Crnojevic-Teodosije-1693
events/Patriarch-Crnojevic-Teodosije-169.content:
Patriarch Arsenije III Crnojević Appoints Teodosije Exarch (21 January 1693)
On 21 January 1693 (10 January Old Style) Patriarch Arsenije III Crnojević of Peć — by then a refugee in Habsburg lands — issued letters at the Lepavina monastery appointing Teodosije as his exarch over the Serbian Orthodox flock in Venetian Dalmatia (doc 262, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The appointment formalised the Serbian church’s jurisdiction over the Kotari migrant population during the Morean War and complements the earlier 1686 Cetinje relocation plan (doc 262, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Patriarch-Pec-Cetinje-Plan-1686.title: Patriarch-Pec-Cetinje-Plan-1686
events/Patriarch-Pec-Cetinje-Plan-1686.content:
Patriarch of Peć’s Cetinje Relocation Plan (December 1686)
In December 1686 the Patriarch of Peć considered relocating his seat to Cetinje and sending 100 cavalry to Stojan Janković in Kotari (doc 160, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The plan attests the Serbian patriarchal hierarchy’s interest in coordinating with Venice’s Morlach commanders during the Morean War, well before the 1693 appointment of Teodosije by Arsenije III Crnojević (doc 160, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Pazin-Peasant-Revolt-1570.title: Pazin-Peasant-Revolt-1570
events/Pazin-Peasant-Revolt-1570.content:
Pazin Peasant Revolt (1570)
Peasant uprising in Pazin County involving ~2,000 subjects, triggered by new wine and feudal taxes imposed across Kranjska, Kras, Vipava, and Pazin Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre. Pazin captain Gaspar-Mauric-b???? reported (4 Sept 1571) that many “Ćići” emigrated back to Ottoman territory (“in die Thurkey”), where authorities resettled them — likely in former Vlasi Istre nahijas in the Sandzak-Klis.

events/Rakoczi-Mission-Vojnovic-1706.title: Rakoczi-Mission-Vojnovic-1706
events/Rakoczi-Mission-Vojnovic-1706.content:
Rákóczi Mission of Baron Vojnović (1706)
In 1706 the Croatian noble Baron Vojnović, an envoy of Ferenc II Rákóczi’s anti-Habsburg insurrection in Hungary, transited through Zadar on his way to Venice and France (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Vojnović’s transit is a brief but illuminating episode of Croatian diplomatic activity in Venetian Dalmatia during the War of the Spanish Succession (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Rama-Franciscan-Migration-1687.title: Rama-Franciscan-Migration-1687
events/Rama-Franciscan-Migration-1687.content:
Rama Franciscan Migration (October 1687)
In October 1687 fifteen friars together with 500+ armed family members fled the San Petar monastery in Rama (central Bosnia) onto Venetian territory; they first settled at Sinj / Dicmo and were eventually placed at the Sustipan abbey near Split (docs 181, 184, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The migration is a foundational moment for the Catholic-Vlach population transferred from Hercegovina/central Bosnia to the Sinj area; frate Andrea, “intrinseco e famigliare” of Mehmed Atlagić, later figured in the Venetian operations against him (docs 181, 184, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II). Compare the contemporaneous Orthodox migration from Skoplje (Uskoplje).

events/Ribnicka-Buna-1702.title: Ribnicka-Buna-1702
events/Ribnicka-Buna-1702.content:
Ribnička buna (1702)
Bunjevac uprising in Lika, also called the Bunjevačka buna, sparked by the conflict between porkulab Milos-Starcevic-b1656-Veliki-Zitnik of Pazariste and vojvoda Marko-Butorac-b????-Lika Saric-2008-Bunjevci.
This is the first major Bunjevac collective political action in recovered Lika, marking them as a “narod koji se mnogo bunio i mnogo selio” in Šarić’s framing. The Starčević lineage that emerges from this episode produces, four generations later, Ante-Starcevic-b1823-Veliki-Zitnik (1823–1896), founder of modern Croatian etnonacionalni identity.
The episode is also the moment when biskup Martin-Brajkovic-b????-Senj of Senjsko-Modruska-Biskupija first uses the term “catholici Valachi alias Bunievczi” in official record (1702) — the first ecclesiastical adoption of the Bunjevac ethnonym.

events/Sinj-Attempt-Marcello-1684.title: Sinj-Attempt-Marcello-1684
events/Sinj-Attempt-Marcello-1684.content:
Failed Sinj Attempt under Marcello (October 1684)
Provveditore Alvise Marcello, supported by Antun Bortulačić, mounted a brief siege of Sinj in October 1684 but withdrew without result (doc 42, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The attempt foreshadowed the much larger Venetian disaster at Sinj in April 1685 and the eventual conquest in September 1686.

events/Sinj-Battle-1685.title: Sinj-Battle-1685
events/Sinj-Battle-1685.content:
Battle of Sinj (7 April 1685)
A Venetian-led assault on Ottoman Sinj that ended in a major Venetian disaster: panic among the Morlachs, rout of the Italian infantry, multiple senior officers killed or captured. The defeat scapegoated provveditor Mocenigo and elevated Pietro Valier (who himself would be replaced by Cornaro the following year).
(docs 33, 38, 39, 40, 42, 60–65, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II)
Killed or missing

Major Tanusi (Oltremarini commander)
Conte Marianović (capitano)
Officer Marušić
Officer Macedonia
Capo Palese of Zadar (spiked the cannon and died defending it)
Colonnello / governator Rados (brother of Ivan Radoš)
Engineer Camuccio (wounded)
Vice ragionato of Valier with 300 cecchini cash
Unnamed Capuchin friar carrying banner of Virgin and brandistocco (boar-spear), presumed enslaved
Ivan Alberti (governator) — captured by Bosnian Pasha, taken as personal slave, ransom letter from Klis

Survived with distinction

Stojan Janković — fought through almost alone among the Morlach capi
Marin Michiel — wounded under his horse; saved by karambaša Nakić’s offered horse
Marchese Carlotti with Valier’s son — last to leave the field

Wider context

Bosnian Pasha advanced from Maidan across the Cetina with cavalry and infantry
Ahmed-paša of Hercegovina simultaneously attacked Kaštela with 3,000 cavalry but was repulsed
The Sinj defeat prevented further Cetina-region operations for the rest of 1685; Venetian initiative shifted to Lika (Lika-Raid-1685) and Kotari migrations (ultimately the Lika-Settlement-Census-1685 roster)

events/Sinj-Conquest-1686.title: Sinj-Conquest-1686
events/Sinj-Conquest-1686.content:
Conquest of Sinj (25–30 September 1686)
Provveditor Generale Girolamo Cornaro took Sinj in a 5-day siege and assault, recovering the seven cannon abandoned in the Venetian disaster of April 1685 and reversing the most painful Venetian defeat of the Morean War to that point (doc 144, 145, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Order of battle (Venetian)

Camp at Salona under Cornaro
General Prince of Parma
General San Polo
Sergente maggior di battaglia marchese dal Borro
Conte Baldassar Spolverino, colonnello (wounded in assault)
Tenente colonnello Pizzamano (later commander of Sinj garrison)
Tenente colonnello Rizzi (distinguished himself)
Tenente colonnello Cittadella (wounded by stone)
Engineer Camuccio
Battery superintendent De Buccò (originally appointed by Valier)
Battery commanders Antonio Loredan (di Zuanne) and Vicenzo Gritti (di Alvise)
Paymaster Lorenzo Zorzi (fu Antonio)
Reinforcements from Makarska under Tranquillo Bollani
Antonio Bollani appointed first provveditore of newly-conquered Sinj

Casualties

Venetian: 25–30 dead, 120+ wounded
Ottoman: 150+ killed in the assault
Recovered: 7 cannon

Aftermath
The Sinj garrison under Pizzamano held off Atlagić’s attempted re-siege in April 1687 (doc 169, relieved by Cornaro and Antonio Zen). Sinj remained Venetian thereafter and was a launching point for the 1687 raids into Hercegovina (Duvno, where Stojan Janković was killed).

events/Sinj-Relief-1687.title: Sinj-Relief-1687
events/Sinj-Relief-1687.content:
Relief of Sinj from Atlagić’s Siege (April 1687)
Cornaro and Antonio Zen marched to relieve Sinj in April 1687 from a siege mounted by Mehmed Atlagić as the new Bosnian pasha; Atlagić withdrew across the Cetina (doc 169, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The relief preserved the Venetian gain from September 1686 and freed the army to launch the summer raids that ended in the death of Stojan Janković at Duvno (doc 169, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Sinj-Siege-Turkish-1686.title: Sinj-Siege-Turkish-1686
events/Sinj-Siege-Turkish-1686.content:
Ottoman Siege of Sinj (April 1686)
A Turkish force besieged Venetian-held Sinj in April 1686; the garrison held off the assault, and Bose Milković mounted an ambush against the besiegers (doc 133, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Sinj remained Venetian and was secured outright in the conquest of September 1686 under Cornaro (doc 133, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Sinobad-Death-Glamoc-1715.title: Sinobad-Death-Glamoc-1715
events/Sinobad-Death-Glamoc-1715.content:
Death of Jovan Sinobad at Glamoč (1715)
Jovan Sinobad, kavalier and sopraintendente of Knin, was killed in an Ottoman engagement at Glamoč in 1715 during the opening campaigns of the Second Morean War (doc 313, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
His death triggered a recall of veterans to active service and reshuffled the senior Kotari command for the rest of the war. He was succeeded eventually by his son Andrea Sinobad as serdar of Knin (doc 313, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Skoplje-Migration-1687.title: Skoplje-Migration-1687
events/Skoplje-Migration-1687.content:
Skoplje (Uskoplje) Orthodox Migration (November 1687)
In November 1687 the Orthodox priest Đurađ led 26 families together with 50 armed men out of the Durakbegović tower in Uskoplje (Hercegovina) onto Venetian territory (doc 183, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The settlers founded the Orthodox enclaves at Dicmo, Biletić and Broćanac on the Venetian-Cetina frontier — the source’s footnote explicitly traces these communities to the 1687 transfer (doc 183, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II). Companion event to the Catholic Rama migration of October 1687.

events/Stojan-Jankovic-Death-Duvno-1687.title: Stojan-Jankovic-Death-Duvno-1687
events/Stojan-Jankovic-Death-Duvno-1687.content:
Death of Stojan Janković at Duvno (23 August 1687)
Per Provveditor Generale Girolamo Cornaro’s dispatch (doc 174, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II), kavalier Stojan Janković was killed at Duvno between 23 and 26 August 1687: struck down by musket and sword while only 8–10 of his companions followed him into the assault — the larger Morlach body refused to advance.
The death ended the most decorated Kotari military career of the Morean War period and marked an inflection point in Venetian Morlach command: his older son Nikola died in the Levant within months, leaving only Konstantin of the named heirs (awarded 10 ducats/month March 1688). The lateral branch through brother Zaviša continued the family’s military leadership into the 1690s.
Notes

Provveditor Generale della Cavalleria Antonio Zen was present in the same campaign; the Duvno operation was part of the wider Cetina–Hercegovina pressure following the conquest of Sinj in 1686.
The refusal of the Morlach body to follow Stojan into the final charge is, in Cornaro’s reading, the visible end of the period in which Morlach loyalty ran through one charismatic leader.

events/Varcar-Vakuf-Raid-1687.title: Varcar-Vakuf-Raid-1687
events/Varcar-Vakuf-Raid-1687.content:
Varcar Vakuf Raid (September 1687)
About 4,000 Morlachs penetrated six days deep into Bosnia toward Varcar Vakuf in September 1687, causing great destruction; Zaviša Janković was wounded in the action (doc 179, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The raid was the family’s first major action after the death of Stojan at Duvno in late August (doc 179, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Venetian-Ottoman-War-1537-1540.title: Venetian-Ottoman-War-1537-1540
events/Venetian-Ottoman-War-1537-1540.content:
Venetian-Ottoman War (1537–1540)
Ottoman capture of Klis fortress (1537) and creation of the Sandzak-Klis under Murat-beg-Gajdic-b????-Sibenik. Venetian siege and capture of Obrovac in June 1538 sparked mass defection of Vlasi-Istre to Venetian territory (Vlasi-Istre-Migration-to-Venice-1538) Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre. Ended with peace 2 October 1540, restoring some Vlach privileges on the Ottoman side and triggering partial return migration.

events/Vid-Petrovic-Banditry-1702-1707.title: Vid-Petrovic-Banditry-1702-1707
events/Vid-Petrovic-Banditry-1702-1707.content:
Vid Petrović’s Banditry on Mt. Prolog (1702–1707)
Vid Petrović of Kosovo (near Sinj) operated as a haiduk on Mt. Prolog from 1702 onward, raiding both Ottoman and Venetian subjects (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
He was killed in 1707 at Bruvno by the agent Canagetti; the son of conte Obradović of Bruvno was killed alongside him (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Vlach-Migration-to-Istria-1518-15.title: Vlach-Migration-to-Istria-1518-1523
events/Vlach-Migration-to-Istria-1518-15.content:
Vlach Migration from Croatia to Istria and Kras (1518–1523)
Several waves of medieval Croatian Vlachs fled northwest ahead of advancing Ottomans, peaking 1518–1523 Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre. Settled hill regions of northern Istria, Kras, and Notranjska. Among them was Tomas-Ruzic-b????-Sibenik (Vodice on Kras, attested 1524) and the Poropat kindred from Buzetski Kras. These would form the demographic core of the later “Vlasi Istre” who returned to Ottoman territory 1528–1530.

events/Vlach-Return-to-Klis-1528-1530.title: Vlach-Return-to-Klis-1528-1530
events/Vlach-Return-to-Klis-1528-1530.content:
Vlach Return Migration to Klis Sanjak (1528–1530)
Under the Ottoman istimâlet policy of Gazi-Husrev-beg and Murat-beg-Gajdic-b????-Sibenik, several hundred Vlach families returned from Habsburg Istria and Kras to their old habitats in Podgorje, Bukovica, and Ravni Kotari Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre. Recorded in the Ottoman mufassal defter 1528–1530 (TR-BOA-TTD No. 157) as Eflâkân-i vilayet-i Istra (“Vlasi zemlje Istre”) — 640 households across 9 nahijas (Ostrovica, Zečevo, Podgorje, Zrmanja, Bukovica, Karin, Obrovac, Benković, Kličevac), in 16 dzemats. Peak settlement before subsequent decline.

events/Vlach-Status-Abolition-1530.title: Vlach-Status-Abolition-1530
events/Vlach-Status-Abolition-1530.content:
Vlach status abolition (c. 1530)
After the Battle of Mohács (1526), Ottoman fiscal pressure for the Hungarian campaigns led to the abolition of special Vlach status and equalization of Vlachs with ordinary raja. The political project failed financially and provoked mass revolts and the first major Vlach migrations out of Ottoman frontier districts Saric-2008-Bunjevci.
Effects on Bunjevac formation

Spring 1530+ — large-scale “uskakanje” (defection) from gornje Pounje, Unac, Glamoč, Grahovo, Knin, and Cetina into Kranjska, Hrvatska, and Zumberak; smaller Vlach streams to Kras in Istria.
1533 — Vlach uprising in the western part of Sandzak-Hercegovina.
1530s+ — Ottoman authorities deported “buntovni vlaški element” from Vilajet-Hrvati to the Podunavlje. A 1564–65 ferman documents one such group permitted to return to its old homeland after ~30 years.

This is the structural backdrop to all of the major Bunjevac migration events that follow (Krmpote-Migration-Lic-1605, Bunjevac-Migration-to-Backa-c1606, etc.).

events/Vlasi-Istre-Migration-to-Venice-1.title: Vlasi-Istre-Migration-to-Venice-1538
events/Vlasi-Istre-Migration-to-Venice-1.content:
Migration of Vlasi Istre to Venetian Territory (1538)
During the Venetian-Ottoman-War-1537-1540, at the urging of providur Alvise-Badoer-b????-Venice, approximately 5,000 Vlachs crossed from Ottoman to Venetian territory in the Zadar hinterland Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre. Led in part by Zakman-Gledjevac-b????-Karin, Petar-Najcinovic-b????-Dobruca-Vas, and the Milovanic and Poropat families. Most were transported by ship via Zadar, Pontadura (Vir), and Ljubač to Istria; ~2,000 families settled there, declining to ~1,700 by 1554 due to harsh ecology and partial return. Captain Nikola-Jurisic-b???? also drew off “Ćići” with 40,000 head of livestock back to northern Istria/Kras.

events/Vrana-Capi-Petition-1684.title: Vrana-Capi-Petition-1684
events/Vrana-Capi-Petition-1684.content:
Petition of Four Morlach Capi to Senate (28 July 1684)
The four Kotari capi — Posedarski, Bortulačić, Janković and Smiljanić — petitioned the Venetian Senate against Provveditore Generale Mocenigo’s appointment of four “new” sub-leaders (Alberti, Soppe, Ventura, Soppe Fortezza), arguing the move violated their established jurisdictions (doc 22, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The Senate ruled in the capi’s favour, confirming their primacy over the Morlach population and rolling back Mocenigo’s appointments (doc 23, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Vrana-Uprising-1683-1684.title: Vrana-Uprising-1683-1684
events/Vrana-Uprising-1683-1684.content:
Vranska buna (October 1683 – May 1684)
The mass mobilisation of Ottoman-subject Morlachi who, on news of the Bečki poraz, in concert with Senjski uskoki and Venetian-side Kotarci, threw off Ottoman rule across the Šibenik–Skradin–Vrana–Obrovac corridor. The volume’s last 80 documents (#321–#399) trace this crisis as Venetian provveditore Lorenzo Donà tries to not declare war while preserving the Morlachi.
Key documents

doc. 321 (1683-10-22) — Posedarski’s first alarm: open insubordination, “viva Christo viva Christo si sono incaminati verso Casich.”
docs. 333, 334 — Šutić’s report; Radoš’s mediation; the Vrana takeover.
doc. 358 (1683-12-26) — pop Lazar Dragović in name of 1500 Morlachi families from Kolašac, Parčić, Krmpote, Rodaljica, Kosulovo Polje, Skradin, Kistanje, Perušić, Benkovac, Brkljača Polača, Mor Polača, who occupied Raslina, Račevica, Dobri Dolac, Dejanović, Putičane, Skonotić, Vrana.
doc. 362 (1684-01-04) — Nakić petition: 1000 Zagora households + 400 Vrana families.
doc. 369 (1684-02-08) — Stojan Janković raised to 40 ducati/month.
doc. 381 (1684-03-01) — Donà’s grand reorganization: 4 direttori (Stojan Janković, Smoljan Smiljanić, Frane Posedarski, Šimun Bortulačić) over the Kotari villages, with named capitanì for each village.
doc. 383 — strength roster of the kotarski + vranski + littoral villages.
doc. 392 (1684-04-09) — Šimun Bortulačić named capo de Morlacchi of Vrana.
doc. 397 (1684-04-19) — Tepšinci/Parčići uskakanje plea (615 fighters / 5307 souls).

Social outcome
Per docs. 381, 397 — the volume closes with the Krajina re-territorialised: the Vrana-Obrovac corridor in Venetian hands, Knin still held by Turks under sandžak Durakbegović, and 5300+ Lika souls poised to migrate to Obrovac and Gračac. The Morean War (1684–99) will start the next month, and the kotarska epopeja will reach its zenith — but that is the subject of Sveska II of Desnica.
People
Stojan Janković, Ilija Mitrović (the principal fomentatore), Smoljan Smiljanić, Frane Posedarski (Younger), Šimun Bortulačić, Bajo Pivljanin, Mitar Pivljanin, Radoš (col. Ivan), Sorić (Stevan, Tepšinci), pop Lazar Dragović, Matija Nakić, Frane Mirčetić, Vid Bačić, Petar Radić, fra Petar Tintić, fra Andrija Rešinčić, fra Grga Šutić.
Turkish side: Durak-beg Durakbegović (who returned to Knin), kapetan Mustaj-beg Firdusović of Knin, alaj-beg Filipović, kliški kajmakam Gazi Mehmed.

events/Vrlika-Capitulation-1688.title: Vrlika-Capitulation-1688
events/Vrlika-Capitulation-1688.content:
Capitulation of Vrlika (early September 1688)
The disdar of Vrlika surrendered the fortress to Fenzi without firing a shot in early September 1688 (doc 216, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
Bože Cerniza placed the new garrison there. The bloodless surrender was a direct consequence of Atlagić’s collapsing position during the simultaneous siege of Knin (doc 216, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/War-of-Spanish-Succession-Deploym.title: War-of-Spanish-Succession-Deployments
events/War-of-Spanish-Succession-Deploym.content:
War of the Spanish Succession — Venetian Morlach Deployments to Italy (1701–1714)
During the War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714) Venice redeployed Dalmatian Morlach formations to Italy, including units led by Zaviša Janković and Lazar Smiljanić (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The Italian deployments stripped the Kotari frontier of seasoned commanders just as the Habsburg-Venetian rivalry over Lika and the 1704 Bukovica revolt heated up (doc text, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Zadvarje-Siege-1685.title: Zadvarje-Siege-1685
events/Zadvarje-Siege-1685.content:
Bosnian Pasha’s Siege of Zadvarje (June 1685)
The Bosnian pasha advanced from the Cetina valley and besieged the Venetian fortress of Zadvarje (Duare) above the Cetina canyon in June 1685; the garrison held until relief arrived (docs 74–78, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The siege came as part of the broad Ottoman counter-offensive of spring–summer 1685 in lower Dalmatia, alongside the Kaštela attack and the Sinj defeat (docs 74–78, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Zagreb-Bishop-Robbery-1688.title: Zagreb-Bishop-Robbery-1688
events/Zagreb-Bishop-Robbery-1688.content:
Robbery of the Bishop of Zagreb (May 1688)
In May 1688 six Kotari Morlachs and two men from Vinjerac ambushed the Bishop of Zagreb as he returned from Rijeka; they took his money and three horses and killed one member of his retinue (doc 203, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The episode prompted Habsburg-Venetian diplomatic friction at a time when the two allies were also competing for Lika settlers (doc 203, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

events/Zavisa-Rebac-Raid-1687.title: Zavisa-Rebac-Raid-1687
events/Zavisa-Rebac-Raid-1687.content:
Zaviša’s Raid on Rebac (June 1687)
Zaviša Janković led 500 men in a raid on Rebac in June 1687 that took 20 horses, 200 cattle and 8 captives (doc 170, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).
The action ran in parallel with his brother Ilija’s raid on Bilaj the same month (doc 170, Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II).

families/Jankovic-Mitrovic.title: Jankovic-Mitrovic
families/Jankovic-Mitrovic.content:
Janković-Mitrović household
Five-brother uskakanje from Ottoman Žegar c. 1647 of which the eldest was Janko Mitrović q. Dimitri. Brought ~70 households / ~150 fighting men into Venetian Ravni Kotari.
Generation 1 (Mitrović)

q. Dimitri Mitrović (father; not himself in the corpus).
Janko Mitrović (eldest; serdar; d. 1659 in Zadar).
Giovanni (Stojan’s supplica doc. 170).
Stefan (ditto).
Pavle (ditto).
Andrija (ditto).
Vukadin Mitrović (probable cousin; d. defending Novigrad 1653).

Generation 2 (Janković, sons of Janko)

Stojan Janković (b. ~1635, d. 1687) — kavalier 1670, capo de Morlacchi 1681.
Sabba Janković — m. Maria Lase 1676.
Ilija Mitrović — bandit; principal fomentatore of the Vrana uprising 1683.
Janja Janković (b. ~1655, d. 1680) — m. Dmitar Nikolić-Pivljanin 1675.

Sons of Vukadin

Jakov Mitrović — slave; pay assigned 1653 then 1681.
Giacomo Mitrović da Islam — 1671 in the Greek-merchant murder case.

Generation 3 (sons of Stojan)
With first wife Vinka/Vuka (d. by 1676):

Zorzi-Alvise Janković b. 1674-04-23 (compare: Battista Sopino).
Anastazija Janković b. 1675.
Nikola Janković — in cavalry.

With second wife Antonia Reci (m. 1676-08-16; Greek of Latin rite of Zadar; daughter of donna Nicolotta and q. Apostolo Rezzi):

Josip Janković b. 1677-09-30.
Konstantin Janković — capitan of 50 fanti from 1679-02-09.

Marriages, in / out

Janja Janković ↔ Mitar Nikolić-Pivljanin (1675) — anchors the Pivljanin line in Zadar.
Wife Vinka — kuma at Bojana Novaković’s baptism (1672).
Stojan Janković ↔ Antonia Reci (1676) — marriage into Zadar Greek-of-Latin-rite milieu.

Religion
Pravoslavni rito greco — Sv. Ilija parohijska crkva u Zadru.
Archive
Arhiv porodice Desnica u Obrovcu — original terminacije on parchment for Janko, Stojan, Vukadin, Jakov; the Trassunto delle benemerenze della famiglia Mitrovich; the 1655 Smiljanić-Zubičević dote document; and other family papers used by Boško Desnica.

families/Smiljanic.title: Smiljanic
families/Smiljanic.content:
Smiljanić household
The Smiljanići were originally from Udbina, not Smiljan in Lika. This is per Desnica’s footnote on doc. 20 of Desnica-1950-Kotarski-Uskoci-I — a definitive correction overriding family-tradition.
Genealogy

Petar Smiljanić (founder; d. 1648-07-17 at Ribnik).

Ilija Smiljanić (d. 1654-09-08 at Vučjak).

Wife Kata (b. Turkish, baptised Christian; remarried Milivoj Zubičević 1655).


Filip Smiljanić (d. Jan 1656 in Šibenik).


(Side branch / nephew of Ilija and Filip):

Smoljan Smiljanić (a/k/a Smoglianovich; also patronymically Mihalevich) — uterine half-brother of Šimun and Marko Brajinović (sons of his mother Anka by her first husband q. Frane Brajinović).

Lazaro Smiljanić (in tenera età 1679) — son.




(Cousin): Bartul Banenović da Pavičići = Germano del carambassà Elia Smiglianich (doc. 66).

Religion
Records do not specify confession; their family arrangements (Kata’s Catholic re-baptism on marriage to Ilija, the Sv. Stošija burial of Filip and his alfier) and the Brajinović Spianata-Sv. Marko residence suggest rito latino.
1671 inheritance restoration
The family-house in Spianata behind Sv. Marko was Anka’s; on Smoljan’s superintendence the silver-bridled saddlery, brocaded vests, gold ornaments, kilims, and weapons were restored to half-brothers Šimun and Marko Brajinović in 1671 (doc. 184 — original document in Arhiv B. Desnice u Obrovcu).

index.title: index
index.content:
Wiki Index
Last updated: 2026-05-02 (Desnica II sweep completed).
Counts: 4 sources · 79 events · 348 places · 483 surnames · 372 persons · 2 families = 1,288 wiki pages.

Sources

Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre — Marko Šarić, “Osmanski Vlasi Istre na izvornoj Tromeđi” (2024). Secondary, scholarly article. Period c. 1500–1585.
Saric-2008-Bunjevci — Marko Šarić, “Bunjevci u ranom novom vijeku” (2008). Secondary, scholarly synthesis on Catholic Vlach Bunjevac formation.
Desnica-1950-Kotarski-Uskoci-I — Boško Desnica, “Istorija kotarskih uskoka 1646–1684, sveska I” (1950). Primary archival anthology of 399 documents — the canonical documentary base for the Kotarski Uskoci.
Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II — Boško Desnica, “Istorija kotarskih uskoka 1684–1749, sveska II” (1951). Primary archival anthology of 392 documents covering the Morean War, Sinj/Knin conquests, Pertinenze reform, and the long Venetian administration through 1749.

Events

Cyprus-War-1570-1573 — Cyprus War; Ottoman capture of Zemunik, Tinj, Vrana
Ottoman-Conquest-of-Croatia-1522-1527 — Conquest creating Vilajet Hrvati
Pazin-Peasant-Revolt-1570 — Drove ~2,000 Ćići back to Ottoman territory
Venetian-Ottoman-War-1537-1540 — War; capture of Klis and Obrovac

people/Aga-Kumalic-b-Udbina.title: Aga-Kumalic-b????-Udbina
people/Aga-Kumalic-b-Udbina.content:
Aga Kumalić
Udbina-area aga. Captured spring 1686 by Zaviša Janković’s četa together with the Udbina disdar Ibrahim-aga and spahija Muhamed-beg, while the latter was supervising agricultural work on his estate (doc. 133, 12 April 1686) Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II.

people/Agostino-Riva-b-Venice.title: provveditor general di Dalmazia
people/Agostino-Riva-b-Venice.content:
Agostino (Đustino) Da Riva
Venetian provveditor general of Dalmatia 1706–1707, successor of Marin Zane. Reported on hajdučija (banditry) at the confines and the death of Vid Petrović at Bruvno 1707 (docs 363, 365) Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II. Received the bishop of Cetinje in 1707 (doc 366). Granted pop Petar Jagodić a salvocondotto (doc 389).
Sources

Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II — docs 362, 363, 364, 365, 366, 389.

people/Ahmed-pasa-Hercegovina-b.title: Pasha of Herzegovina
people/Ahmed-pasa-Hercegovina-b.content:
Ahmed-paša (of Hercegovina)
Pasha of Hercegovina; commanded a 3,000-cavalry attack on Kaštela (Trogir coast) April 1685, doc 62 Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II. Defeated by 3,000 castellani plus Morlaks.
Sources

Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II — doc 62.

people/Alberto-Fortis-b.title: padovanski redovnik / etnograf
people/Alberto-Fortis-b.content:
Alberto Fortis (1778)
Italian-Padovan friar and naturalist. First to record the Buna-river origin legend of the Bunjevci in the appendix to the English edition of his Viaggio in Dalmatia (London, 1778), describing the inhabitants of the Velebit coast Saric-2008-Bunjevci (Fortis 1984:276–277):

Stanovnici planina danas su posve različiti od onoga što su tada bili. Sami sebe nazivaju Bunjevcima, jer su došli s područja Bune u Bosni…

His attestation marks the moment when the legend of Buna-origin entered the European etnografska literature. Šarić’s structural argument: this is a legend in 18th-c. literary recording, not a 16th-c. historical narrative — its real origin is Bosanska franjevačka provincija pastorally-jurisdictional propaganda.

people/Alessandro-Molin-b-Venice.title: provveditor generale in Dalmazia
people/Alessandro-Molin-b-Venice.content:
Alessandro Molin (Molino)
Venetian patrician; provveditor generale in Dalmazia 1689–1692, between Girolamo Cornaro and Daniel Dolfin Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II (docs 226–242, 257).
Major acts in this source

Jan 1690 — Appointed Cesare Casanova capitan/governator of Obrovac; dismissed Filippo Mitrović as captain of a 56-foot Obrovac company Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II (docs 226, 227).
Jan 1690 — Established the salt scale at Obrovac Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II (doc 226).
Feb 1690 — Granted 10 ducats/month to vladika Visarion Borilović of Cetinje for promoting Venetian interests in Montenegro Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II (doc 232).
Feb 1690 — Granted lands of the Krka monastery of Sv. Arhangel (San Michiel Arcangelo) to the Greek-rite monks Don Giuseppe Zavalac and Stefan Janoški Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II (doc 231).
1690 — Divided the Kotari into Upper Kotari (Mitrović serdarstvo) and Lower Kotari (Milković serdarstvo) — appointed Zaviša Mitrović and Bože Milković serdari respectively Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II.
24 May 1690 — Appointed Jovan (Zuanne) Sinobad governor of Zvonigrad with a 50-paesano company; salary 14 ducats Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II (doc 234).
June 1691 — Appointed Filippo Sinobad capitano of Zvonigrad to replace his brother Jovan, who was simultaneously promoted to governor of Knin krajina with 60 fields & vineyards near Bulin Most plus houses in Knin from late Turks Hadži Kurtović, Hadži Emorić, Ahmet-aga Livaković Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II (docs 239, 240, 241).

Notes

Refused to meet Ilija Mitrović when Ilija fled Obrovac upon Molin’s arrival in 1690 (doc 228) Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II.
Succeeded by Daniel Dolfin in February 1692.

people/Alexandro-Bondumier-b-Venice.title: kapetan mletačke fuste
people/Alexandro-Bondumier-b-Venice.content:
Alexandro Bondumier
Captain of a Venetian fusta. Spring 1532: arrested an Ottoman-subject Morlach smuggler between Dalmatia and Istria, seizing 6 horses and 300 ducats Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre.

people/Alija-sin-Poropata-b-Karin.title: Alija-sin-Poropata-b????-Karin
people/Alija-sin-Poropata-b-Karin.content:
Alija, sin Poropata
Muslim convert of the Poropat kindred; recorded in selo Karin in 1528 Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre.

people/Alvise-Badoer-b-Venice.title: providur Dalmacije
people/Alvise-Badoer-b-Venice.content:
Alvise Badoer
Venetian providur of Dalmatia. Architect of the 1538 transfer of ~5,000 Vlachs from Ottoman territory (“Banadego”) to Venetian Zadar contado, recognizing their military value Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre.

people/Alvise-Barbaro-b-Venice.title: trogirski knez
people/Alvise-Barbaro-b-Venice.content:
Alvise Barbaro
Trogirski knez (1588). Recommended to the Senate that Vlach defectors from Ottoman territory be sent directly to Istria Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre.

people/Alvise-Marcello-b-Venice.title: Venetian noble
people/Alvise-Marcello-b-Venice.content:
Alvise Marcello
Venetian nobleman who led the failed October 1684 Sinj attempt together with Šimun Bortulačić, doc 42 Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II.
Sources

Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II — doc 42.

people/Alvise-Mocenigo-II-b-Venice.title: provveditor general di Dalmazia (1696–1702); Doge of Venice
people/Alvise-Mocenigo-II-b-Venice.content:
Doge Alvise Mocenigo II
Provveditor general of Dalmatia 1696–1702 (succeeding Daniel Dolfin); subsequently became Doge of Venice. Signed ducale of 22 March 1702 (doc 342) and others (docs 345, 360, 380) Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II.
A dukal of 20 August 1705 (doc 360) granted the hereditary count title to Ilija, Nicolò and Stojan Janković (Mitrović).
A later dukal of 1 December 1729 removed Petar Mitrović-Stojisavljević and named Giacomo Sinobad serdar of Knin (doc 380).
Sources

Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II — docs 305 et seq., 342, 345, 360, 380.

people/Alvise-Pasqualigo-b-Venice.title: Provveditor general (interim authority Oct 1684)
people/Alvise-Pasqualigo-b-Venice.content:
Alvise Pasqualigo
Venetian Provveditor general; held interim authority in October 1684 (doc 41) Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II. Also doc 43.
Sources

Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II — docs 41, 43.

people/Alvise-Renier-b-Venice.title: bailo
people/Alvise-Renier-b-Venice.content:
Alvise Renier
Venetian bailo at Constantinople (early 1550). Reported that Morlaci Istrijani on Zadar territory served as informants for the Senj uskoks Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre.

people/Andrea-Civran-b-Venice.title: providur Dalmacije
people/Andrea-Civran-b-Venice.content:
Andrea Civran
Venetian providur of Dalmatia. July 1524: reported to the Council of Ten on Tomas-Ruzic-b????-Sibenik’s contacts with Gazi-Husrev-beg Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre.
Distinct from Antonio-Civran-b????-Venice, kapetan gulfa active 1615 (Krmpote relacija) — likely a same-family successor.

people/Andrea-Michiel-b-Venice.title: Capitano of Zadar (1684)
people/Andrea-Michiel-b-Venice.content:
Andrea Michiel
Venetian noble; Capitano of Zadar in 1684, doc 33 Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II. Distinct from Polo-Michiel-b????-Venice and Marin-Michiel-b????-Venice.
Sources

Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II — doc 33.

people/Andrija-Frletic-b-Dracevac.title: uskok kapetan
people/Andrija-Frletic-b-Dracevac.content:
Andrija Frletić (“Andre kapetan”)
Son of a Dracevac Muslim convert; among the most famous Senj uskok captains of the late 16th c., remembered in epic tradition as “Andre kapetan” Saric-2024-Vlasi-Istre. Brother of Vuk.

people/Andrija-Josip-Mandal-b-Lika.title: vojni svećenik
people/Andrija-Josip-Mandal-b-Lika.content:
Andrija Josip Mandal (1733)
Vojni svećenik for all of Lika and Krbava. In his 1733 izvješće he no longer calls Bunjevci Vlachs but says they are similia (in dress, customs, life) to Vlachs (Burić 2002:132) Saric-2008-Bunjevci.
Marker for the moment when vlaški drops out of the official designation in Senjsko-Modruska-Biskupija and only Bunjevac remains, after biskup Martin-Brajkovic-b????-Senj introduced the dvojni naziv “catholici Valachi alias Bunievczi” in 1702.

people/Andrija-Kacic-Miosic-b.title: fra, pjesnik
people/Andrija-Kacic-Miosic-b.content:
fra Andrija Kačić Miošić (1756)
Bosanski franjevac, pjesnik. Author of Razgovor ugodni naroda slovinskoga (Zagreb, 1756) — celebrates Bunjevac military lineages of the Senjska-Kapetanija / Lika area as “vitezovi hrvatski” Saric-2008-Bunjevci (Kačić Miošić, Razgovor ugodni, “Pisma druga od vitezova hrvatskih…“):

Ali evo zmaja ognjenoga / po imenu Starčević Jakova!

Names alongside Jakov-Starcevic-b????-Pazariste: Balenovići, Došeni, Milinkovići, Rukavine. Šarić takes Kačić’s mid-18th-c. attribution of “hrvatsko ime” to all prekovelebitski junaci as evidence of the regional/military Hrvati identity already taking root in Bunjevac kin by the time of the Lika regiment’s formation Saric-2008-Bunjevci.

people/Andrija-Sinobad-b-Posedarje.title: captain of Zvonigrad company; later serdar of Knin
people/Andrija-Sinobad-b-Posedarje.content:
Andrea (Andrija) Sinobad
Son of kavalier Jovan Sinobad. Appointed captain of the Zvonigrad company in 1697 as a child (with a tutor governatore assigned), on his father’s merit (doc 304) Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II. Later served as serdar of Knin; died in 1725 (referenced 1726, docs 376, 378). Cousin Giacomo Sinobad later succeeded as serdar of Knin in 1729.
Sources

Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II — docs 304, 376, 378.

people/Angelo-Emo-b-Venice.title: Conte (count/governor) of Zadar (1684)
people/Angelo-Emo-b-Venice.content:
Angelo Emo
Venetian noble; Conte (governor) of Zadar in 1684, doc 33 Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II.
Sources

Desnica-1951-Kotarski-Uskoci-II — doc 33.

people/Ante-Starcevic-b1823-Veliki-Zitni.title: politician, writer
people/Ante-Starcevic-b1823-Veliki-Zitni.content:
Ante Starčević (1823–1896)
Born in Veliki-Zitnik near Pazariste in Lika — direct descendant of the Bunjevac porkulab Milos-Starcevic-b1656-Veliki-Zitnik, šukununuk-level. Founder of modern Croatian etnonacionalni identity through the Hrvatska stranka prava (HSP).
Šarić cites the Starčević lineage as the paradigmatic case of the transformation: in just one century, an “influential bunjevačka obitelj” went from Bunjevac to “snažan hrvatski identitet.” Cousins David Starčević and Mile Starčević continued the political project Saric-2008-Bunjevci.
Šime Starčević was Ante’s stric (uncle).

people/Anto-Matkovic-b-Temisvar.title: fra (Bosanska franjevačka provincija)
people/Anto-Matkovic-b-Temisvar.content:
fra Anto Matković (1582)
Bosnian Franciscan who in 1582 opened a school for “Dalmatince” in the Temišvar diocese (Bušić 2005:51) Saric-2008-Bunjevci.
“Dalmatinci” in Hungarian-Catholic terminology = the Bunjevac/štokavski-ikavski population transferred to Podunavlje from the Klis-area Ottoman frontier — same demographic substrate later named Bunievczi in the 1622 Kaloča petition of Simun-Matkovic-b???? (likely a relative).

people/Anto-Ripcanin-b.title: fra (dušobrižnik Morlaka)
people/Anto-Ripcanin-b.content:
fra Anto Ripčanin (1670–71)
